definition: Colloquial term for a heterosexual person or orientation.
notes: Used across clinical and casual registers interchangeably; also has many non-sexual meanings, making contextual disambiguation necessary in corpus work.

definition: Informal abbreviation for bisexual, denoting attraction to more than one gender.
notes: Fully mainstream abbreviation; used in both identity and descriptive senses with no residual stigma in most English-speaking contexts.

definition: Informal abbreviation for pansexual, denoting attraction to people regardless of gender.
notes: Common in LGBTQ+ subculture and among younger demographics; the distinction from 'bi' is debated within communities; recognition drops sharply in older cohorts.

definition: Informal abbreviation for asexual, denoting little or no sexual attraction to others.
notes: The playing-card ace is used as a symbol by asexual communities; recognition is growing but still substantially subculture-bound.

definition: Informal abbreviation for aromantic, denoting little or no romantic attraction to others.
notes: Less widely known than 'ace'; primarily circulates within ace/aro community spaces; the romantic/sexual distinction it relies on is itself a relatively recent conceptual framework.

definition: Experiencing little or no romantic attraction to others, distinct from asexuality which concerns sexual attraction.
notes: The romantic/sexual attraction distinction is a conceptual development of the 2000s–2010s; the term is semi-clinical in community use and growing in mainstream awareness.

definition: Public health acronym for 'men who have sex with men,' categorizing sexual behavior irrespective of identity.
english_term: men who have sex with men
notes: Deliberately behavior-based rather than identity-based; developed for HIV/STI epidemiology to capture men who do not identify as gay or bisexual but engage in same-sex behavior; not widely known outside public health or research contexts.

definition: Public health acronym for 'women who have sex with women,' categorizing behavior irrespective of identity.
english_term: women who have sex with women
notes: Appears less frequently in research literature than MSM; same behavior-first framing; recognition is very low outside public health and academic contexts.

definition: Term used primarily in religious and conservative contexts for a person who experiences same-sex attraction without adopting a gay or lesbian identity.
notes: Preferred in some religious frameworks (e.g. celibate gay Catholic, ex-gay adjacent) to describe experience while resisting identity-label politics; also appears in Australian clinical literature with a more neutral valence; the phrase deliberately separates attraction from identity.

definition: Having a gender identity that shifts or varies over time rather than remaining fixed.
notes: Term rose to mainstream awareness in the mid-2010s; broadly recognized though acceptance and interpretation vary significantly across political and generational lines.

definition: Identifying as having no gender or as existing outside of gender entirely.
notes: Distinct from nonbinary (which acknowledges a gender, just not a binary one); recognition is growing but still primarily within LGBTQ+ and online communities.

definition: Describing a person who practices or is open to consensual romantic or sexual relationships with multiple partners simultaneously.
notes: Adjectival form of polyamory; both terms surged in mainstream recognition in the 2010s–2020s; distinct from swinging in its emphasis on emotional intimacy alongside or instead of recreational sex.

definition: The practice of having consensual romantic or sexual relationships with multiple partners simultaneously.
notes: Coined circa 1990; Greek/Latin hybrid portmanteau (polys + amor); distinct from polygamy (not marriage-based, gender-neutral); distinct from swinging (emphasis on relationships, not just sex).

definition: Maintaining a sexual or romantic relationship with only one partner at a time.
notes: The cultural and legal default in most Western societies; used in clinical, legal, and casual registers without distinction; increasing use in contrast with polyamory discourse.

definition: Having multiple spouses simultaneously; typically illegal in Western jurisdictions but practiced in some religious and cultural communities.
notes: Technically encompasses polygyny (one man, multiple wives) and polyandry (one woman, multiple husbands); in common English usage almost always implies polygyny; carries varying moral weight depending on cultural context.

definition: A person who engages in consensual partner-swapping or group sexual activity with other couples.
notes: Term became culturally prominent in the 1960s–70s; still active and broadly recognized; distinct from polyamory in its typical emphasis on recreational sex over emotional intimacy; associated with a recognizable subculture with its own venues.

definition: The practice of consensual partner-swapping or group sex among couples, typically as a recreational lifestyle.
notes: Activity-noun form of swinger; the lifestyle aspect distinguishes it from one-off encounters; still maintains a distinct subculture separate from the newer polyamory community.

definition: A romantic partnership in which both parties have agreed that sexual or romantic activity with others outside the relationship is permitted.
notes: Broad umbrella term encompassing swinging, polyamory, and don't-ask-don't-tell arrangements; widely understood across generations; less subculture-specific than either 'polyamory' or 'swinging.'

definition: A man whose partner has sex with other men; historically a term of humiliation and social shame, now also used for the consensual kink practice involving erotic arousal from the same scenario.
notes: Derived from cuckoo bird behavior; the abbreviation 'cuck' had a spike as a political insult circa 2016; kink usage remains active online; the term straddles the honor/shame economy and kink categories depending on era and context.

definition: The state or practice of being a cuckold; in modern use, the consensual kink in which a man's erotic arousal derives from his partner's sexual activity with other men.
notes: More formal and archaic noun form than 'cuckold' or 'cucking'; appears in historical literature and academic or kink-community writing; the -ry suffix gives it a quasi-clinical or literary register.

definition: A married woman who has sex with men other than her husband with his full knowledge and enthusiastic consent, framed as a source of shared erotic pleasure.
notes: Distinct from cuckoldry in framing: hotwife arrangements emphasize the wife's desirability and the husband's pride and arousal rather than humiliation; recognized within CNM and kink communities; primarily an internet-era subculture term.

definition: In the stag/vixen kink dynamic, the husband or male partner who takes confident pride in facilitating and watching his wife's sexual activity with other men.
notes: Used in the 'stag/vixen' pairing as an explicit alternative framing to cuckold; emphasizes confidence and pride rather than humiliation; very niche, primarily found in online kink forums; 'stag' has many common non-sexual meanings that swamp this usage in general corpora.

definition: A person who derives sexual pleasure from watching others engaged in intimate or sexual behavior.
notes: French loanword (voyeur, 'one who sees'); clinical use implies non-consensual watching (DSM voyeuristic disorder); kink use may be fully consensual; the word is broadly understood in general culture and has a neutral-to-titillating register in lay usage.

definition: A person who derives sexual pleasure from exposing themselves or performing sexually in front of others.
notes: Clinical term spanning both DSM exhibitionistic disorder (non-consensual exposure) and consensual kink exhibitionism; also used metaphorically for attention-seeking behavior in non-sexual contexts, which slightly dilutes the sexual signal in general corpora.

definition: A person who derives sexual arousal from both inflicting and receiving pain, humiliation, or domination.
notes: Portmanteau of sadist (from Marquis de Sade) and masochist (from Leopold von Sacher-Masoch); abbreviated S&M or SM; largely subsumed into the broader BDSM framework in contemporary kink discourse, making 'sadomasochist' feel slightly clinical or dated compared to 'into BDSM.'
